title: Peer Memory (Person + Department)
markdown:
An external, peer-keyed memory layer gives the Executive durable cross-channel recall, sitting on top of Honcho via `openexecutive.memory.honcho_client`. The `HONCHO_ENABLED` env var gates it; when false every entry point short-circuits with `outcome=disabled` and behavior matches the pre-Honcho posture.

### Two scopes

- **Per-person**, keyed by `Person.id` — a user chatting from Discord, Telegram, email, or web is one peer card, so facts shared in any channel surface in the others. Each entry point resolves the caller to a `Person.id` (channel-ID lookups for adapters; `x-caller-email` for web).
- **Per-department**, keyed by `department_<slug>` — each department accumulates an institutional voice from dept-scoped decisions, advice, committee outcomes, and dept-bound specialist turns.

### Flow

`prefetch` runs once per turn, calling Honcho's dialectic endpoint and injecting a `<peer_memory>` block into the user turn (empty on timeout). `prefetch_department` does the same per consulted specialist that maps to a department, yielding `<department_memory>`. After the response, `sync_turn` and `sync_department_turn` persist the exchange as fire-and-forget background tasks that never block the user.

### Prefetch budget

The budget is `HONCHO_PREFETCH_TIMEOUT_S` **scaled by the requested `reasoning_level`** (`minimal`/`low` 1.5x, `medium` 3x, `high` 4x, `max` 5x), then capped at an absolute ceiling and never taken below the configured base. Honcho's dialectic latency scales steeply with that level — roughly 2s at `low` against 8s at `medium` — so a single flat budget made the deeper levels unreachable: every `medium` call (the committee path, and inbound email, which defaults to committee review) timed out and the turn silently ran with no peer memory at all, which is strictly worse than having asked for `low`. `minimal` shares `low`'s multiplier rather than taking the bare base, because it measured *slower* than `low` and is the default for the standard per-turn path. The ceiling exists because `prefetch` is awaited inline before the first streamed byte, so scaling must not turn a generous base into user-visible dead air. Each prefetch audit row records the `timeout_s` it ran under.

The SDK client's own HTTP timeout is an **outer** bound, kept strictly greater than every per-call budget — never equal to the prefetch budget, which used to silently cap `directional_chat` below its 30s ceiling.

### Peer identity

Peers are keyed by `Person.id`, so the only identity signal Honcho gets from the key alone is a bare integer — and its dreaming agent concludes that the number *is* the person's name (observed in production as a card reading `IDENTITY: Name: 1`). Because cards are injected into the dialectic system prompt on every `chat()`, that error propagates into every later answer about that person. So both sync paths seed each person peer's card from the roster, for the sender, the department-turn originator, and co-present peers alike.

The card carries the **name only** — email and role would export roster PII to a third-party memory service, including for people who were merely cc'd, and neither is needed to fix the defect. `set_card` replaces the whole card, so only `IDENTITY:` lines are swapped (matched case- and whitespace-insensitively) and the deriver's own `ATTRIBUTE:` / `RELATIONSHIP:` lines survive. Roster values are flattened to a single line, length-capped, and **refused outright if they carry a card structure token** — `upsert_person` is a chat tool, so a roster value is attacker-reachable and would otherwise be able to forge card lines inside a system prompt.

Seeding runs *after* the message write (persisting the exchange is the point of the sync and must not queue behind two card round trips per peer), is bounded per peer, and is best-effort. It is memoized per `(workspace, person)` on the facts sent, with a recheck interval — a roster rename re-seeds immediately, and because the deriver keeps re-deriving identity from the peer id, a one-shot memo would let `IDENTITY: Name: 1` come back unnoticed.

### Cross-pollination & isolation

When a person turn touches a department, the dept peer joins the person's session as a co-present peer — the hybrid peer graph that lets later queries synthesize across both timelines, with synthesis depth degrading at greater peer-graph distance. Demo fixtures run in a sacrificial `openexec-fixture-<name>` workspace so demo turns never pollute real peer cards. Every wrapper call emits a `peer_memory` audit row (`op` + `outcome`) into the per-turn flow at `/audit/session/{id}`.
